newsitem.title: JAPAN: Highlights of Japan securities panel's report.
newsitem.headline: Highlights of Japan securities panel's report.

text.p: Following are the main points of an interim report released by Japan's Securities and Exchange Council, an advisory panel to the finance minister.

The interim proposals, contained in more than 50 pages, were compiled by three working groups within the advisory panel and the council is scheduled to finalise its proposals next month to help Japan set a schedule for implementing its "Big Bang" reforms of financial markets.
The final report will be automatically adopted by the ministry, financial sources said.
The interim report's proposals were as follows:
-- Japan should move swiftly to liberalise commissions on stock transactions in order to complete deregulation well before 2001
-- initially, stockbroking-fee liberalisation should cover only stock transactions above a threshold set at less than 100 million yen so as to smooth the transition to a deregulated environment.
-- tax authorities should consider abolishing securities transaction taxes to improve the efficiency of Japan's securities markets and to cut trading costs to internationally competitive levels.
-- securities houses should be allowed to start offering multi-service accounts to enable customers to transfer profits automatically from stock sales into money management funds.

-- securities houses should be allowed to offer "wrap" accounts, widely used in the United States, in which a securities house manages an investor's assets based on discretionary management contracts or by introducing third-party advisory firms to investors.
-- mechanisms should be enshrined in the law to prevent customers losing their money if deregulation pushes brokerages into bankruptcy.
-- transactions involving listed stocks should be allowed outside Japan's eight stock exchanges in order to step up competition.

-- harsher penalties should be imposed against illegal stock transactions in line with global standards, and staff numbers should be increased at Japan's securities watchdog, the Securities and Exchange Surveillance Commission (SESC), to improve its market-monitoring operations.
-- rules which restrict brokers from engaging in business such as asset management, investment trusts, insurance and commodities futures should be abolished.
-- financial institutions, such as banks, should be allowed to start over-the-counter sales of investment trusts so as to make Japan's investment trust funds more attractive to investors.
-- introduction of privately placed investment trusts should be permitted for a limited number of investors.
